name: FeedFast
tagline: Hosted feedback board where users post and upvote feature requests, plus a changelog to close the loop.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Strip the marketing away and a feedback board is a form, a vote counter, a status column, and a public page. None of those need a vendor, and the data is yours by definition: it is your own users talking about your own product. The genuinely fiddly parts are vote deduplication without forcing logins, spam filtering, and an embeddable widget that does not look glued on, and an agent will get you 80 percent of each in an afternoon. The thing you are actually buying is not being the person who maintains yet another public-facing web app. Verdict is yes on capability, with the honest caveat that public detail on this particular product is thin, so treat the comparison as category-level.
coreLoopDIY: A public board where anyone can submit a request, upvote it once, and watch it move through statuses, with an admin view behind a token and a changelog feed when things ship.
requirements: a place to host a small Node app
a domain or subdomain if you want it public
optional SMTP credentials if you want status-change emails
whatYouLose: Real spam and brigading defence: your board will get hit by bots the week it ranks for anything
Identity-based vote dedupe, so cookie plus IP hashing is the best you get without logins
Email notifications, digests, and the automatic nudge when a request ships
A drop-in embed widget that matches your app instead of looking like an iframe from 2014
Integrations that push requests into Linear, Jira, or Slack without you writing the glue
moatNotes: The polish is in the anti-abuse and the embed, not in the CRUD. Everything else is a table with a vote count.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a feedback board is public infrastructure with your logo on it, and the failure modes are embarrassing rather than invisible: duplicate spam at the top of the list, a broken embed on your pricing page, an upvote button that lets one person vote four hundred times. Paying converts a small ongoing maintenance obligation into a line item, and for a solo founder that trade is often correct even when the build is trivial. The data is not a moat here, so you can leave whenever you want, which is the healthiest kind of subscription.
notes: Cheap to build, mildly annoying to own. That is the whole product category.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted public feedback board and changelog. Empty folder, start from scratch.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) with Tailwind CSS
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/feedback.db, schema created on boot
- No external services, no auth provider, no analytics, no telemetry

Public pages:
- / : board listing requests, sortable by votes or newest, filterable by status (open, planned, in-progress, shipped, declined)
- A submit form: title, body, optional email, honeypot field, simple rate limit of 3 submissions per IP hash per hour
- One upvote per request per visitor, deduped by a signed cookie plus a hash of IP and user agent; clicking again removes the vote
- /r/[id] : single request page with comments (name optional, same rate limiting)
- /changelog : reverse-chronological entries with markdown body, rendered server side
- /changelog/rss : valid RSS 2.0 feed of changelog entries

Admin:
- /admin protected by a single ADMIN_TOKEN in .env, checked against an httpOnly cookie set at /admin/login
- Admin can edit or delete requests and comments, change status, merge two requests (votes and comments move to the target), and write changelog entries
- When a request moves to shipped, show a one-click action to draft a changelog entry prefilled with its title

Also include:
- /embed.js that injects a fixed-position "Feedback" button opening the submit form in an iframe, origin configurable via .env
- Seed script with 12 fake requests and 2 changelog entries
- README with setup, .env.example (ADMIN_TOKEN, COOKIE_SECRET, PUBLIC_ORIGIN, SITE_NAME), and a single npm run dev command

Explicitly out of scope: email notifications, user accounts, SSO, multi-project support, Linear or Jira sync, payment. Do not stub them, do not leave TODOs for them.
Store all IP-derived values as salted hashes only. Never log raw IPs.
